newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan stocks seen punching past 10,000.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan stocks seen punching past 10,000.

text.p: Taiwan's red hot stock index on Monday challenged yet another threshold -- 10,000 points -- extending a sustained assault that some analysts say may not ease until it yields an all-time high close.

Powered by a sizzling high-technology sector and good growth prospects in other industries, the benchmark index surged within five points of its first five-digit close in seven years, but failed to muster enough momentum for a final push above 10,000.

The index finished at 9,923.05, a gain of 0.55 percent or 53.80 points that prompted some experts to say it would brush aside political concerns and eclipse -- in 1997 -- its record high close of 12,495.34, dating to February 10, 1990.
"Maybe some of the gains are speculative, but the fact is that Taiwan's economy is good enough to justify the gains," said Allen Huang, fund manager for National Securities.
"There is really nothing that can stop the index from setting a new record high by the end of this year," he said.
Despite the late fade, Monday's close was the highest since the index ended at 9,978.86 on April 12, 1990, and analysts widely concur that resistance at 10,000 will dissipate soon.

The economy broke out of a 1995-6 slump by posting strong 6.83 percent gross domestic product growth in the first quarter. The government forecasts full-year GDP growth at 6.24 percent -- far exceeding the 5.71 percent of 1996.

High-tech shares have been the driving force behind a rough doubling of the main index in the 16 months since rival China's military menacing of Taiwan sent stock market funds fleeing into foreign exchange, gold and other havens.

The sector, powered by computer giant Acer and chipmaking blue chip Taiwan Semiconductor, rose a whopping 111 percent in the first half of 1997 and is widely tipped to enjoy sizzling second half sales.
Analysts say the tech-sectors sales surge would come from Intel Corp's aggressive pricing of its market-leading Pentium microprocessors in 1997.

"If Pentium prices go down, Taiwan's computer companies will see a dramatic increase in sales, which in turn will bring additional business for integrated circuit firms," said Wang Jieh, analyst for Foremost Investment Services.
"It's all a cycle that starts with Intel at the top and trickles down to related industries," Wang said.
Intel, the world's largest microprocessor maker, on Sunday slashed Pentium prices by up to 50 percent, and said it would cut prices again in November.

Aside from electronics, analysts said several government-led infrastructure projects -- like the southern Tainan science park and a T$442 billion bullet train project -- would pump life into the long-sagging construction industry.
"The projects will encourage more domestic investment and keep private capital from leaving the island," Foremost's Wang said.

The science park, already being built, has commitments from Taiwan Semiconductor and rival chipmaker United Microelectronics to invest T$400 billion or more each in world-class computer wafer production lines.
The trans-island rail project has attracted rival consortium bids led by China Development Corp, a venture capital firm backed by the ruling Nationalist Party, and Continental Engineering.
The government has vowed to pick a contractor in November.

On the political front, analysts said a long chill in Taiwan's ties with arch rival China -- whose sabre-rattling sank the index to a political nadir of 4,692.40 on March 12, 1996 -- was unlikely to sap the market this time around.

"With their Communist Party congress coming up (in October) and Hong Kong's recent handover, the Chinese communists will not have too much energy to target Taiwan," said Lin Long-hsien, senior analyst for United Securities.
"At least for this year, the stock market will continue to focus on economic factors," Lin said.
